items.question: A machine was bought on 1 April 2026 for ₹6,00,000. Installation cost was ₹40,000. Estimated useful life is 5 years and estimated residual value is ₹40,000. Using the straight line method, annual depreciation is:
items.explanation: Depreciable amount is cost (purchase price plus installation) less residual value. Dividing this by the useful life gives the annual straight line charge.

why_not.A: Left out installation cost but still deducted residual value.
why_not.C: Added residual value to cost instead of deducting it.

items.exam_tip: Depreciable amount = cost including installation minus residual value. Divide by life only after that.

items.question: A machine costing ₹5,00,000 was bought on 1 April 2025. Estimated useful life is 5 years and residual value is ₹50,000. Using the straight line method, what is the book value of the machine on 31 March 2027?
items.explanation: Annual depreciation under SLM = (cost - residual value) / life = ₹4,50,000 / 5 = ₹90,000. After 2 years, accumulated depreciation is ₹1,80,000. Book value = ₹5,00,000 - ₹1,80,000 = ₹3,20,000.

why_not.B: Ignored residual value: used ₹5,00,000/5 = ₹1,00,000 a year, giving ₹3,00,000.
why_not.C: Deducted only one year of depreciation (₹90,000) and so got ₹4,10,000 is avoided; this is cost less 1.5 years' error.
why_not.A: Deducted only one year's depreciation of ₹90,000, giving ₹4,10,000 as book value.

items.exam_tip: Book value = cost less accumulated depreciation. Residual value is removed only when finding yearly depreciation.
items.reviewer_note: Option C (₹3,50,000) is not tied to a clean error; its why_not text is vague. Consider replacing C with ₹3,95,000 or a clearer distractor, e.g. ₹4,50,000 (depreciable amount only).

items.topic: Ind AS 16 Property, Plant and Equipment
items.question: On 1 July 2026, Rudra Ltd bought a machine with list price ₹20,00,000 less 10% trade discount. GST of 18% is fully recoverable as input credit. It paid freight ₹30,000, installation ₹20,000 and testing cost ₹15,000. Initial operating loss was ₹40,000. What is the cost of the machine?
items.explanation: Cost includes purchase price net of trade discount and directly attributable costs: freight, installation and testing. Recoverable GST and initial operating losses are not part of cost under Ind AS 16.

why_not.D: Adds initial operating loss of ₹40,000, which Ind AS 16 says is not capitalised.
why_not.C: Ignores the trade discount and takes the full list price.
why_not.A: Adds recoverable GST to cost, though input credit is not a cost of the asset.

items.exam_tip: Capitalise: net price plus directly attributable costs. Exclude: recoverable taxes, initial operating losses, admin overheads.
check_notes: Checker: Minor: the question does not say whether the testing cost is a cost of checking that the asset functions properly, which is what makes it capitalisable.
Checker: Minor: the question does not say that the machine was ready for use on 1 July 2026.

items.question: A factory budgets overheads of ₹6,00,000 and 80,000 direct labour hours for FY 2026-27. Actual overheads are ₹5,98,000 and actual hours worked are 78,000. Overheads are absorbed on direct labour hour rate. Find the under/over absorption.
items.explanation: Absorption uses the budgeted rate on actual hours. Rate ₹7.50 × 78,000 hours = ₹5,85,000 absorbed. Actual overhead ₹5,98,000 is higher, so ₹13,000 is under-absorbed.

why_not.B: Reverses the sign; absorbed is less than actual, so it is under-absorbed.
why_not.D: Compares budgeted and actual overhead only, ignoring the hours actually worked.
why_not.C: Subtracts absorbed overhead from budgeted overhead instead of actual overhead.

items.exam_tip: Absorbed = budgeted rate × actual base. Absorbed less than actual means under-absorbed.

items.question: On 30 September 2026, Mehta Ltd holds a semi-finished item costing ₹5,00,000. Its estimated selling price after completion is ₹5,40,000. Further cost to complete is ₹25,000 and estimated selling cost is ₹30,000. At what amount should it be carried under Ind AS 2?
items.explanation: Ind AS 2 requires inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value. NRV is selling price less cost to complete and cost necessary to make the sale. NRV ₹4,85,000 is below cost ₹5,00,000, so the item is written down.

why_not.B: Kept cost; ignored that NRV is lower than cost, so no write-down made.
why_not.D: Deducted only the cost to complete and forgot the selling cost.
why_not.C: Deducted only the selling cost and forgot the cost to complete.

items.exam_tip: NRV = selling price - cost to complete - selling costs. Then take the lower of cost and NRV.

items.question: The risk-free rate is 7% p.a. and the expected return on the market portfolio is 13% p.a. A share has a beta of 1.2. As per CAPM, what is the required rate of return on this share?
items.explanation: CAPM: Ke = Rf + β × (Rm − Rf). Market risk premium is 13% − 7% = 6%. Beta-adjusted premium is 1.2 × 6% = 7.2%. Adding the risk-free rate gives 14.2%.

why_not.A: Forgot to add the risk-free rate; this is only the beta-adjusted risk premium.
why_not.B: Multiplied beta by market return (1.2 × 13%) and ignored the risk-free rate.
why_not.D: Used Rf + β × Rm instead of β × (Rm − Rf), double counting the risk-free rate.

items.exam_tip: Beta multiplies the risk premium (Rm − Rf), never Rm alone. Then add Rf back.
